chunks: As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Ghiyāth, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said:
There is no harm in the blood of fleas and bedbugs, and in the urine of bats.

The correct approach regarding this narration is that we interpret it as a form of taqiyyah, because it conflicts with the foundational principles of the madhhab. For we have already explained that everything whose flesh is not lawful to eat, salat is not valid in its urine; and the bat is among those whose flesh is not eaten, so salat is not valid in its urine. The first narration explicitly confirms these principles.

key_terms.أُصُولِ الْمَذْهَبِ: the foundational principles of the legal school
key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary conformity employed in particular circumstances
key_terms.الرِّوَايَةُ: the transmitted report or hadith narration
key_terms.بَوْلِهِ: its urine, the substance under discussion in the ruling

ai.seo_question: How does al-Istibsar treat the narration about the urine of bats in relation to salat?
ai.summary: This passage cites a hadith stating that there is no harm in the blood of fleas and bedbugs and the urine of bats, then explains that the report concerning bat urine is to be understood as taqiyyah. The ruling is aligned with the established Shia legal principle that salat is not valid in the urine of animals whose flesh is not lawful to eat.
